fix.after: _read_until_settled(path): read once; if it parses to an object -> accept (no pause). Else loop up to 4x { sleep(0.2); re-read; if readable -> return settled; track moved/quiet }. At exhaustion: moved or still moving -> status 'unstable' (SKIP + reason); never moved -> 'settled' -> error is reported as a HARD failure. audit() now also returns skip_reason, retried and docs (so no caller re-reads a moving file).
fix.justification: 200 ms is ~3 orders of magnitude longer than the time a 16-23 KB handoff write needs to become visible, so 'identical across reads' stops meaning 'identical across one syscall gap'. The bound is deliberately small because it is a LATENCY budget, not a correctness one: exhaustion while a file is MOVING is a skip, so a slow writer is never punished for outliving the window, and a file that never moved is a settled defect at 0.8 s exactly as it was at 0 ms. Only SUSPECT (unparseable) files pay the pause - the live corpus paid ZERO pauses (retried == [] over 177 handoffs, 9 of them known baseline gaps), so the suite does not crawl (5 consecutive full-file runs: 13 passed in 2.44 s each).
fix.docstring_before: 'A committed broken handoff is stable across two reads, so it is still caught; a torn read is not, so the guard does not flicker.'
fix.docstring_after: CORRECTED, not merely re-worded: 'THE OVERSTATEMENT THIS CORRECTS (U8.35). The old claim -- "a torn read is not [stable], so the guard does not flicker" -- was too strong, for exactly V8.29's reason ... The loop does NOT remove that exposure and this docstring no longer says it does; no finite window can outlast a writer that pauses longer than the window. What IS now true: the window is a real pause instead of two back-to-back syscalls, and a file that MOVES at all during the watch can never become a hard failure. SETTLE_DELAY_S and SETTLE_MAX_ATTEMPTS are therefore a LATENCY budget, not a correctness one.'

tightenings.shapes_param: retired: _regressions(gaps, shapes, baseline) -> _regressions(gaps, baseline). The parameter was never read (callers had already filtered gaps by shape), so it invited the reader to believe a shape filter happened inside. All 3 call sites updated.
tightenings.weak_assertion: tightened, without coupling to a version-fragile literal. Before: assert "line 6 column 32" in err or "delimiter" in err. After: err = failures[0]["error"]; assert err.startswith("JSONDecodeError: "), err; assert "delimiter" in err, err. The old form accepted EITHER a position literal that CPython renumbers between releases (the brittle half) OR a bare substring (the weak half, satisfiable by any unrelated message). Both facts are now required and neither is a position pin; the frozen fixture's real message is "JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 6 column 32 (char 1165)", which satisfies the tightened conjunction.

next_unit_hint: The loop is a latency budget, not a correctness one: the residual exposure is a tear that stays frozen (byte-identical to every read) for longer than the whole 0.8 s window, which is still reported as a settled defect, and a tear that leaves VALID but incomplete JSON, which parses on the first read and is accepted. Both are recorded in the module docstring rather than papered over; a verifier should treat a 9/1-style run as evidence about WINDOW SIZE, not about a defect, and should re-read the corpus file after a delay before believing any red.
